result.rationale: The diff clearly shows parseRefreshTokenResponse doing `if (!refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token) { refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"; }`, and callers (Google CalendarService, Zoom VideoApiAdapter, Office365, Salesforce) persist the parsed result directly to prisma.credential.update. So a response legitimately omitting refresh_token would get the literal string 'refresh_token' stored as the credential's refresh token, breaking subsequent refresh attempts. The mechanism is verifiable in the diff.

judged_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse overwrites a missing refresh_token with the literal placeholder string "refresh_token" before the credential is persisted. Any integration whose refresh response legitimately omits refresh_token gets a fake refresh_token persisted, so the next real refresh attempts to use the string 'refresh_token' as an OAuth grant and fails — the placeholder should flow through the sync path only, not be written into stored credentials.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, the function mutates the parsed token payload by setting `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` whenever it is missing. Call sites can then persist this value: e.g. `Office365CalendarService` does `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };` after calling `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...)`, so if the refresh response omits `refresh_token`, the placeholder overwrites the real stored refresh token and will be written back to Prisma in the subsequent `prisma.credential.update(...)`. This can break subsequent refreshes by using the literal string "refresh_token" as the grant.
